claim: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) is a powerful technology used to define the spatial distribution and relative abundance of metabolites across tissue cryosections.
source: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) is a powerful technology used to define the spatial distribution and relative abundance of metabolites across tissue cryosections.
evidence: This is a general statement about MSI technology that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The research community lacks an easy computing and application tool that images any metabolite abundance ratio pairs.
source: While software packages exist for pixel-by-pixel individual metabolite and limited target pairs of ratio imaging, the research community lacks an easy computing and application tool that images any metabolite abundance ratio pairs.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in available tools, based on the authors' assessment of existing software capabilities.

claim: Recognition of correlated metabolite pairs may contribute to the discovery of unanticipated molecules in shared metabolic pathways.
source: Importantly, recognition of correlated metabolite pairs may contribute to the discovery of unanticipated molecules in shared metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential benefits of metabolite ratio analysis.

claim: An untargeted R package workflow for pixel-by-pixel ratio imaging of all metabolites detected in an MSI experiment has been developed.
source: Here, we describe the development and implementation of an untargeted R package workflow for pixel-by-pixel ratio imaging of all metabolites detected in an MSI experiment.
evidence: This describes the primary contribution of the manuscript - the development of new software.

claim: Ratio imaging minimizes systematic data variation introduced by sample handling.
source: Considering untargeted MSI studies of murine brain and embryogenesis, we demonstrate that ratio imaging minimizes systematic data variation introduced by sample handling, markedly enhances spatial image contrast, and reveals previously unrecognized metabotype-distinct tissue regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing ratio and non-ratio imaging approaches.

claim: Ratio imaging markedly enhances spatial image contrast.
source: Considering untargeted MSI studies of murine brain and embryogenesis, we demonstrate that ratio imaging minimizes systematic data variation introduced by sample handling, markedly enhances spatial image contrast, and reveals previously unrecognized metabotype-distinct tissue regions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative images shown in the manuscript.

claim: Ratio imaging reveals previously unrecognized metabotype-distinct tissue regions.
source: Considering untargeted MSI studies of murine brain and embryogenesis, we demonstrate that ratio imaging minimizes systematic data variation introduced by sample handling, markedly enhances spatial image contrast, and reveals previously unrecognized metabotype-distinct tissue regions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing novel tissue regions identified through ratio imaging.

claim: Ratio imaging facilitates identification of novel regional biomarkers.
source: Furthermore, ratio imaging facilitates identification of novel regional biomarkers and provides anatomical information regarding spatial distribution of metabolite-linked biochemical pathways.
evidence: This is demonstrated through examples in the manuscript showing biomarker discovery.

claim: Ratio imaging provides anatomical information regarding spatial distribution of metabolite-linked biochemical pathways.
source: Furthermore, ratio imaging facilitates identification of novel regional biomarkers and provides anatomical information regarding spatial distribution of metabolite-linked biochemical pathways.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and spatial mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The algorithm is applicable to any MSI dataset containing spatial information for metabolites, peptides or proteins.
source: The algorithm described herein is applicable to any MSI dataset containing spatial information for metabolites, peptides or proteins, offering a potent hypothesis generation tool to enhance knowledge obtained from current spatial metabolite profiling technologies.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the method based on its design principles.

claim: Recent developments in mass spectrometry imaging enable spatial mapping at or near cellular resolution.
source: Recent developments in mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) enable spatial mapping of the relative distribution and abundances of proteins, peptides, lipids, small molecule metabolites, drugs and elemental isotopes in heterogeneous tissue sections (Shimma, 2022) with resolution at, or near, cellular (Zhang et al., 2023a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: MSI has become a promising tool in the era of spatial-omics.
source: Hence, MSI has become a promising tool in the era of spatial-omics (Zhang et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2023; Soudah et al., 2023; Sivanesan et al., 2023; Rončević et al., 2023; Moore et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Ikegawa et al., 2023; Gorman et al., 2024; Gitta et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2022), especially at the single cell level (Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: MALDI, SIMS, and DESI are the dominant modes of ionization for MSI.
source: Matrix-assisted laser desorption and ionization (MALDI), secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), and desorption electrospray ionization (DESI) are the dominant modes of ionization for MSI.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the MSI field.

claim: All MSI analyses provide pixel-by-pixel relative abundances of all detected charged molecular masses regardless of ionization method, pixel size, and knowledge of structural identity.
source: Regardless of ionization method, pixel size, and knowledge of structural identity, all MSI analyses provide pixel-by-pixel relative abundances of all detected charged molecular masses.
evidence: This describes a fundamental characteristic of MSI data.

claim: Current MSI data processing tools are mainly limited to relative abundance data only.
source: Current MSI data processing tools provide 2D or 3D image data visualization as heatmaps from normalized pixel-by-pixel data of acquired mass spectra (Vos et al., 2021; Verbeeck et al., 2020; Alexandrov, 2012; Trede et al., 2012) and are mainly limited to relative abundance data only.
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing MSI software tools.

claim: Metabolite ratio imaging has been used in medical MRI spectroscopy to study metabolite distribution within tissue.
source: Metabolite ratio imaging has been used in medical MRI spectroscopy to study metabolite distribution within tissue (Riches et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SIMS ratio imaging has been used in biological, material, and environmental sciences.
source: SIMS ratio imaging has been used in biological, material, and environmental sciences (Jia et al., 2023; Pumphrey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Targeted serum and urine metabolite ratios have aided assessment of genome-wide GWAS and MWAS association of metabolic traits by serving as proxies for enzymatic reaction rates.
source: Additionally, targeted serum and urine metabolite ratios have aided assessment of genome-wide GWAS and MWAS association of metabolic traits by serving as proxies for enzymatic reaction rates (Suhre et al., 2011; Illig et al., 2010; Gieger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior GWAS/MWAS studies.

claim: Hypothesis-free testing of ratios between all possible metabolite pairs in tissue extracts analyzed by GWAS and MWAS have provided an innovative approach for discovery of new biologically meaningful molecular associations.
source: Hypothesis-free testing of ratios between all possible metabolite pairs in tissue extracts analyzed by GWAS and MWAS have provided an innovative approach for discovery of new biologically meaningful molecular associations (Petersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Metabolite ratios have been used to construct large-scale neural networks that improve statistical assessments and facilitate data interpretation.
source: Furthermore, metabolite ratios have been used to construct large-scale neural networks that improve statistical assessments and facilitate data interpretation (Lassen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Several free and commercially available software packages are available for band ratio computation and imaging in geographical and hyperspectral imaging.
source: In geographical and hyperspectral imaging, several free and commercially available software packages are available for band ratio computation and imaging.
evidence: This is supported by listing specific software tools with URLs.

claim: Existing hyperspectral imaging tools can perform an individual ratio image from an input pair, but may require additional programing to image ratios from the untargeted metabolite pairs in an MSI dataset.
source: The above four tools can perform an individual ratio image from an input pair, but may require additional programing to image ratios from the untargeted metabolite pairs in an MSI dataset (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This identifies a limitation of existing tools that the current work addresses.

claim: Pixel-by-pixel imaging of the ratio of an enzyme's substrate to its derived product may offer an opportunity to view the distribution of functional activity for a given metabolic pathway across tissue.
source: While individual ion abundances in spatial metabolite profiling fail to inform on metabolic pathway activity, or on the identity of metabolic intermediates contributing to these pathways, pixel-by-pixel imaging of the ratio of an enzyme's substrate to its derived product may offer an opportunity to view the distribution of functional activity for a given metabolic pathway across tissue.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the utility of ratio imaging for pathway analysis.

claim: Brain and adipose tissues from COX10 knockout and wildtype mice were frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until processing.
source: Brain and adipose tissues from a mitochondrial myopathy model of cytochrome c oxidase assembly factor heme A:farnesyltransferase COX10 knockout (COX10 KO) and wildtype (WT) mice were frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until processing.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation methods used in the study.

claim: Mouse decidua dissected from pregnant females at gestation day 8.5 were embedded in 2% carboxymethylcellulose.
source: Entire mouse decidua dissected from pregnant females at gestation day 8.5 were embedded in 2% carboxymethylcellulose, frozen in liquid nitrogen, stored at –80 °C, and sectioned at 12 µm nominal thickness.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation methods for embryo samples.

claim: Brain cryosections were cut at 10 µm thickness.
source: Brain cryosections (n=4 per group) were cut at 10 µm and adipose at 20 µm thickness (n=3 for wildtype control and n=4 for COX 10 KO), mounted on conductive slides coated with indium tin oxide (ITO; Delta Technologies; cat # CB-90IN-S111) and stored at –80 °C.
evidence: This describes the sectioning parameters used in the study.

claim: Adipose cryosections were cut at 20 µm thickness.
source: Brain cryosections (n=4 per group) were cut at 10 µm and adipose at 20 µm thickness (n=3 for wildtype control and n=4 for COX 10 KO), mounted on conductive slides coated with indium tin oxide (ITO; Delta Technologies; cat # CB-90IN-S111) and stored at –80 °C.
evidence: This describes the sectioning parameters used in the study.

claim: NEDC matrix was used for murine brain and E8.5 embryos.
source: On the day of MALDI MS data acquisition, ITO-slides with tissue sections were transferred to a vacuum chamber and dried for 30 min prior to deposition of desired matrices for imaging: N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (NEDC; 10 mg/ml in 75% methanol) for murine brain and E8.5 embryos; 1,5-diaminonaphthalene (DAN, 2 mg/mL in 50% acetonitrile) for murine COX10 KO adipose tissues, and 9-aminoacridine (9AA, 5 mg/ml in 85% Ethanol) for murine hippocampus.
evidence: This describes the matrix selection for different tissue types.

claim: DAN matrix was used for murine COX10 KO adipose tissues.
source: On the day of MALDI MS data acquisition, ITO-slides with tissue sections were transferred to a vacuum chamber and dried for 30 min prior to deposition of desired matrices for imaging: N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (NEDC; 10 mg/ml in 75% methanol) for murine brain and E8.5 embryos; 1,5-diaminonaphthalene (DAN, 2 mg/mL in 50% acetonitrile) for murine COX10 KO adipose tissues, and 9-aminoacridine (9AA, 5 mg/ml in 85% Ethanol) for murine hippocampus.
evidence: This describes the matrix selection for different tissue types.

claim: 9-Aminoacridine matrix was used for murine hippocampus.
source: On the day of MALDI MS data acquisition, ITO-slides with tissue sections were transferred to a vacuum chamber and dried for 30 min prior to deposition of desired matrices for imaging: N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (NEDC; 10 mg/ml in 75% methanol) for murine brain and E8.5 embryos; 1,5-diaminonaphthalene (DAN, 2 mg/mL in 50% acetonitrile) for murine COX10 KO adipose tissues, and 9-aminoacridine (9AA, 5 mg/ml in 85% Ethanol) for murine hippocampus.
evidence: This describes the matrix selection for different tissue types.

claim: MALDI MSI data were acquired at raster width of either 10 µm or 80 µm using a 7T scimaX-MRMS mass spectrometer.
source: MALDI MSI data were acquired at raster width of either 10 µm or 80 µm using a 7T scimaX-MRMS mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics, USA) equipped with a SmartBeam II laser and a MALDI source.
evidence: This describes the instrumentation and acquisition parameters.

claim: Compound identifications were assigned based on both accurate mass (<2 ppm mass accuracy) and isotope pattern matches to free source metabolite and lipid databases.
source: Compound identifications were assigned based on both accurate mass (<2 ppm mass accuracy) and isotope pattern matches to free source metabolite and lipid databases, including the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), KEGG and LIPIDMAPs.
evidence: This describes the metabolite identification approach.

claim: Missing values are annotated with 1/5 the minimum value quantified in all pixels in which a metabolite was detected.
source: Towards this, we first obtain the minimum abundance of a particular m/z among all pixels with detectable abundance (i.e. excluding missing values), then use 1/5 this minimum value as a threshold to annotate missing value.
evidence: This describes the missing value imputation strategy used.

claim: The R codes for ratio imaging are available on GitHub.
source: Notably, a series of SCiLS lab API R codes for ratio imaging visualization, data analysis, and UMAP segmentation are available for download on GitHub (https://github.com/qic2005/Untargeted-mass-spectrometry-ratio-imaging copy archived at qic2005, 2024).
evidence: This provides information about code availability.

claim: R codes are available to extract pixel data directly from .imzml file using Cardinal 3.0 free-source software.
source: For MSI data acquired from other non-Bruker MS imaging instruments, R codes are also available to extract pixel data directly from.imzml file, a common data format for MS imaging, using Cardinal 3.0 free-source software and the resulting pixel data can be applied for ratio imaging (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the compatibility of the approach with different data formats.

claim: Ratio imaging does not require absolute metabolite quantification.
source: Although stable isotope standards and mimetic tissue model are often used to obtain quantitative concentration of metabolite/lipid of interest, it is not applicable for untargeted metabolite ratios that include an assessment of structurally undefined species. Note that the utilization of our strategy is to provide untargeted (and targeted) ratio imaging as a hypothesis generation tool and our quantification data indicate this use does not require absolute metabolite quantification.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of abundance-based and concentration-based ratio images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Similar ratio images are obtained from abundance data compared to quantified concentration data for lactate, glucose, and ascorbate.
source: To test this, we quantify the absolute concentration of brain glucose, lactate, and ascorbate using stable isotope standards spiked into the mimetic tissue sections prepared from carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) embedded brain homogenate. Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows similar ratio images among lactate, glucose, and ascorbate obtained from abundance data compared to quantified concentration data.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data comparing abundance and concentration ratios.

claim: Pixel-by-pixel ratioing of metabolite/feature pairs reduces artefacts caused by non-uniform matrix coating of cryosections.
source: Pixel-by-pixel ratioing of metabolite/feature pairs offers the important advantage of reducing artefacts caused by non-uniform matrix coating of cryosections and other elements of sample processing, especially for slides containing multiple tissue cryosections.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative images in Figure 2.

claim: Individual cryosections undergo varying degrees of metabolically-active metabolite degradation at typical –20 °C cryotome operating temperature.
source: This is because as tissue cryosections are thaw-melted onto slides individually, the layout sequence results in variable waiting times for completion of the mounting process. Thus, individual cryosections undergo varying degrees of metabolically-active metabolite degradation, even at the typical –20 °C cryotome operating temperature.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of tissue handling effects and inference about metabolite stability.

claim: LPEs with polyunsaturated acyl chains of 20:4, 22:4, and 22:6 predominantly originate from PLA1 action.
source: Notably, LPEs with polyunsaturated acyl chains of 20:4, 22:4, and 22:6 shown in Figure 2 predominantly originate from PLA1 action.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of phospholipase specificity.

claim: 20:4 and 22:4 acyl chains are derived from the ω6 fatty acids arachidonic acid and adrenic acid.
source: Note that 20:4 and 22:4 acyl chains are derived from the ω6 fatty acids arachidonic acid (AA) and adrenic acid, whereas 22:6 acyl chains originate from an ω3 fatty acid, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about fatty acid classification.

claim: 22:6 acyl chains originate from an ω3 fatty acid, docosahexaenoic acid.
source: Note that 20:4 and 22:4 acyl chains are derived from the ω6 fatty acids arachidonic acid (AA) and adrenic acid, whereas 22:6 acyl chains originate from an ω3 fatty acid, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about fatty acid classification.

claim: Ratio images of LPE 20:4 and LPE 22:4 to LPE 22:6 show enhanced brain structure with markedly sharper definition compared to diffuse non-ratio images of individual LPEs.
source: Compared to diffuse non-ratio images of individual LPEs, the ratio images of ω6 to ω3 LPEs show an enhanced brain structure with markedly sharper definition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing images in Figure 2A-C with Figure 2D-F.

claim: Overall LPE ratios were unchanged between COX10 KO and WT genotypes despite variable LPE values imaged between genotypes.
source: Despite variable LPE values imaged between COX10 KO and WT brains, overall LPE ratios were unchanged between genotypes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the imaging data presented.

claim: For a given enzyme, pixel-wise specific enzyme activity may be inferred from pixel-by-pixel ratio imaging of substrate-product metabolite pairs.
source: For a given enzyme, pixel-wise specific enzyme activity may be inferred from pixel-by-pixel ratio imaging of substrate-product metabolite pairs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the interpretation of ratio imaging data.

claim: Comparison of pathway activity can only be limited to the equivalent pixel/regions of tissues from different biological groups, given the assumption that ionization efficiency is identical for equivalent pixel from different tissue sections.
source: However, due to differences in ionization efficiency, comparison of pathway activity can only be limited to the equivalent pixel/regions of tissues from different biological groups, given the assumption that ionization efficiency is identical for equivalent pixel from different tissue sections (i.e. same cell type and microenvironment).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the approach based on ionization efficiency considerations.

claim: Enhanced glycolytic activity was seen in the amnion and visceral yolk sac of E8.5 embryos.
source: Consistent with a role for the visceral yolk sac in providing nutrients, including glucose for embryo development, enhanced glycolytic activity was seen in the amnion and visceral yolk sac (Figure 3A-B).
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Higher abundances of FA 18:1 relative to FA 18:0 are predominantly located in the allantois, head mesenchyme, and especially in the hindbrain neuroepithelium.
source: Furthermore, higher abundances of the desaturase product FA 18:1 relative to FA 18:0 (reflecting SCD activity) and of phophatidylethanolamine (PE) 38:4 relative to LPE 18:0 (reflecting PLA2 activity) are predominantly located in the allantois, head mesenchyme, and especially in the hindbrain neuroepithelium for FA 18:1 to FA 18:0 (Figure 3C-H).
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PLA1 and PLA2 appear to have quite different compartmented activities among yolk sac, amnion, and head mesenchyme.
source: Interestingly, PLA1 and PLA2 appear to have quite different compartmented activities among yolk sac, amnion, and head mesenchyme (Figure 3G-H).
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neurons have higher ATP/ADP, ADP/AMP, IDP/IMP ratios in mouse hippocampus.
source: In accord with this expectation, higher ATP/ADP, ADP/AMP, IDP/IMP ratios (Figure 3J–L) are observed in neurons of mouse hippocampus, while indicators of oxidative stress (Figure 3I) and fatty acid synthesis (Figure 3P) were unchanged in neurons compared to other cell types.
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Elevated SCD and AMPD activities were predominantly observed in neurons compared to other cell types in mouse hippocampus.
source: Elevated SCD and AMPD activities were also predominantly observed in neurons (Figure 3M–N) compared to other cell types, consistent with SCD being a novel regulator of neuronal cell proliferation and differentiation and their reported immunocytochemical results (Knecht et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neurons display a relatively lower level of DHA (ω3) to AA (ω6) fatty acids vs. other cell types in mouse hippocampus.
source: Although a higher ratio of ω3 to ω6 fatty acids predicts improved hippocampus-dependent spatial memory and cognitive status in older adults (Andruchow et al., 2017), ratio imaging surprisingly shows that these neurons display a relatively lower level of DHA (ω3) to AA (ω6) fatty acids vs. other cell types in mouse hippocampus.
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 3 and contrasts with expectations from cited literature.

claim: COX10 KO mice are typified by decreased white adipose stores, accelerated lipolysis with increased free fatty acid deposition and low leptin levels with decreased food intake.
source: We previously reported that COX10 KO mice are typified by decreased white adipose stores, accelerated lipolysis with increased free fatty acid deposition and low leptin levels with decreased food intake (Southwell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on prior published work by the authors.

claim: COX10 KO adipose tissue shows decreased abundance ratio of FA 22:6 (DHA, ω3 fatty acid) to FA 20:4 (AA, ω6 fatty acid).
source: As expected, distinct fatty acid and lipid profiles point to altered ω3 (DHA) to ω6 (AA) fatty acid composition (Figure 4A), fatty acid and lipid desaturation (Figure 4B–G), fatty acid synthesis (Figure 4H–J) and phospholipid hydrolysis (Figure 4K–L) in KO vs. WT adipose.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratio imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lower adipose ω3 to ω6 ratios have been associated with inflammation.
source: Lower adipose ω3 to ω6 ratios have been associated with inflammation (Bakker et al., 2023), obesity (Pinel et al., 2021), altered gut microbiota (Portela et al., 2023; Wall et al., 2009) and other health problems (Chiusolo et al., 2023; Rix et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The diminished ω3 to ω6 ratio in COX10 KO mice may arise from an altered gut microbiome.
source: These ratio imaging findings led us to speculate that the diminished ω3 to ω6 ratio in COX10 KO mice arises from an altered gut microbiome, supported by unpublished preliminary findings.
evidence: This is a speculation based on ratio imaging findings and preliminary unpublished data.

claim: Supplementation of human COX10 mutant patients with ω3 fatty acids may effectively modify the microbiome to restore normalized adipose tissue composition and food intake.
source: This emergent hypothesis from ratio imaging analysis raises the clinically important possibility that supplementation of human COX10 mutant patients with ω3 fatty acids may effectively modify the microbiome to restore normalized adipose tissue composition and food intake.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis generated from the ratio imaging findings.

claim: Pixel-by-pixel metabolite ratio imaging almost invariably resolves distinct tissue structures and uncovers fine structure and anatomically unrecognized regions not revealed by individual metabolite imaging alone.
source: In contrast, pixel-by-pixel metabolite ratio imaging almost invariably resolves distinct tissue structures but also uncovers fine structure and anatomically unrecognized regions not revealed by individual metabolite imaging alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple examples in the manuscript.

claim: Individual glutamate, aspartate and glutamine distribution images failed to show a clear structural distribution in COX10 KO and WT mouse coronal brain sections.
source: Using COX10 KO and WT mouse coronal brain sections as an example, we observed that individual glutamate, aspartate and glutamine distribution images failed to show a clear structural distribution, (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by images shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Ratio imaging revealed a 1.59-fold increase in aspartate to glutamate ratio in an unusual 'moon arc' region across the amygdala and hypothalamus relative to the rest of the coronal brain.
source: However, ratio imaging revealed a 1.59-fold increase in aspartate to glutamate ratio in an unusual 'moon arc' region across the amygdala and hypothalamus (mean abundance 0.563 in 6345 pixels) relative to the rest of the coronal brain (mean abundance 0.353 in 45742 pixels, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of ratio imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Glutamate to glutamine ratio shows a 1.63-fold increase in intensity in an arc-like structure within the ventral thalamus and hypothalamus compared to the rest of the brain.
source: Similar but different arc-like structures are encompassed within the ventral thalamus and hypothalamus, wherein glutamate to glutamine ratio show a 1.63-fold increase in intensity compared to the rest of the brain (mean abundance of 0.695 in 7108 pixels vs 0.428 in 44979 pixels, Figure 5E), while relative glutamine to aspartate abundance appears enriched in the striatum (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of ratio imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Enrichments of aspartate to glutamate and glutamine to glutamate near the thalamus, nucleus accumbens and hypothalamus were robust and consistently reproduced in MALDI-MSI experiments using an independent cohort of COX10 KO and WT mouse brains.
source: Note that the enrichments of aspartate to glutamate and glutamine to glutamate near the thalamus, nucleus accumbens (NAc) and hypothalamus (and visualization of their reciprocal ratio images) were robust and consistently reproduced in MALDI-MSI experiments using an independent cohort of COX10 KO and WT mouse brains (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This demonstrates reproducibility of the findings across independent experiments.

claim: Enrichment of glutamate to aspartate in the cortex region was confirmed in horizontal and sagittal brain sections from random mouse brains.
source: Enrichment of glutamate to aspartate in the cortex region was further confirmed in horizontal and sagittal brain sections from random mouse brains (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This demonstrates reproducibility across different section orientations.

claim: Aberrations in glutamate, glutamine, and aspartate homeostasis are all implicated in neurological disease.
source: Considering the above, it is notable that aberrations in glutamate, glutamine, and aspartate homeostasis are all implicated in neurological disease (Hertz and Rothman, 2017; Andersen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Aspartate serves as an amino donor for glial glutamate formation.
source: Aspartate serves as an amino donor for glial glutamate formation (Pardo et al., 2011), and the hippocampal aspartate to glutamate ratio has been related to changes in brain glucose (Szerb and O'Regan, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The glutamate-glutamine cycle is closely linked to cellular energy metabolism.
source: The glutamate-glutamine cycle is closely linked to cellular energy metabolism (Andersen et al., 2022), and ratios between neurotransmitters (GABA, glutamine, and glutamate) have been used in MRS studies to probe neurological disease mechanisms and progression (Kantorová et al., 2022; Kantorová et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ratios among glutamine, glutamate, and aspartate have been implicated in memory function, schizophrenia, depression, alcoholism and motivated performance via NAc.
source: Specifically, ratios among glutamine, glutamate, and aspartate have been implicated in memory function (Limón et al., 2021), schizophrenia, depression, alcoholism and motivated performance via NAc (Hangel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondrial myopathy alters glutamine, glutamate and aspartate signaling near the NAc.
source: In COX10 KO and WT brains, differential aspartate to glutamate and glutamine to glutamate ratios point to an interesting linkage between muscle health and brain neurotransmitter signaling: mitochondrial myopathy alters glutamine, glutamate and aspartate signaling near the NAc.
evidence: This is inferred from the ratio imaging data showing differences between COX10 KO and WT brains.

claim: Unknown non-ratio metabolite feature data in a given ROI can be combined with known metabolite ratios, pixel-by-pixel, to discover correlations between unknowns and metabolite ratios that inform on a specific enzyme activity or metabolic pathway.
source: Unknown non-ratio metabolite feature data in a given ROI can be combined with known metabolite ratios, pixel-by-pixel, to discover correlations between unknowns and metabolite ratios that inform on a specific enzyme activity or metabolic pathway.
evidence: This describes a potential application of the ratio imaging approach.

claim: The unknown [M-H] 375.23059 was negatively correlated with the ratios of PA 36:4 to LPA 16:0 and PA 36:1 to PA 18:1 in COX10 KO and WT mouse adipose.
source: Using COX10 KO and WT mouse adipose as an example, the unknown [M-H] 375.23059 was negatively correlated with the ratios of PA 36:4 to LPA 16:0 and PA 36:1 to PA 18:1, indicating that the abundance of this unknown metabolite may be positively associated with PLA1 and/or PLA2 activity (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The unknown [M-H] 375.23059 could be a reduction product of CPA 16:0 after loss of one oxygen atom, matching the formula C19H37O5P with 0.013 ppm mass accuracy.
source: Indeed, direct correlation of this unknown with lipid metabolites suggests it could be a reduction product of CPA 16:0 after loss of one oxygen atom, matching the formula C19H37O5P with 0.013 ppm mass accuracy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on correlation analysis and accurate mass matching.

claim: Calculating the Spearman correlation of combined pixel data from both individual metabolites and metabolite ratios revealed an unexpected positive association of FeCl2 with the glutamate to glutamine ratio in COX10 KO and WT mouse brain sections.
source: Another example of correlation-based discovery comes from consideration of COX10 KO and WT mouse brain sections, where calculating the Spearman correlation of combined pixel data from both individual metabolites and metabolite ratios revealed an unexpected positive association of FeCl2 with the glutamate to glutamine ratio, along with other related metabolite ratios that include aspartate, NAA, glucose and glutathione (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Free iron is recognized as a key mediator of glutamate excitotoxicity in spinal cord motor neurons.
source: Notably, free iron is recognized as a key mediator of glutamate excitotoxicity in spinal cord motor neurons (Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Significant associations between peripheral markers of iron metabolism and glutamate with glutamine in relation to total creatine concentration have been reported in female human brains.
source: Significant associations between peripheral markers of iron metabolism and glutamate with glutamine in relation to total creatine (Glx:tCr) concentration have been reported in female human brains (Burger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Glutamate facilitates divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) flux and subsequent increases in brain free iron content.
source: Glutamate facilitates divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) flux and subsequent increases in brain free iron content (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Decreased FeCl2 levels in combination with decreased glutamate in the cortex region of COX10 KO vs. WT brain is an unexpected finding.
source: Decreased FeCl2 levels in combination with decreased glutamate in the cortex region of COX10 KO vs. WT brain is an unexpected but intriguing finding.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the imaging data.

claim: Aging is associated with increased brain iron through cortex-derived expression of the iron regulatory hormone hepcidin.
source: While aging is associated with increased brain iron through cortex-derived expression of the iron regulatory hormone hepcidin (Sato et al., 2022), calorie restriction down-regulates hepcidin expression (Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calorie restriction down-regulates hepcidin expression.
source: While aging is associated with increased brain iron through cortex-derived expression of the iron regulatory hormone hepcidin (Sato et al., 2022), calorie restriction down-regulates hepcidin expression (Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: COX10 KO mice exhibited decreased food intake and adopted a metabolic state resembling caloric restriction.
source: In accord with decreased Fe2+ and glutamate to glutamine ratio, COX10 KO mice exhibited decreased food intake and adopted a metabolic state resembling caloric restriction (Southwell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on prior published work by the authors.

claim: Most segmentation approaches rely on unsupervised clustering algorithms that can readily result in the generation of biologically unrealistic tissue structures.
source: Most segmentation approaches rely on unsupervised clustering algorithms that can readily result in the generation of biologically unrealistic tissue structures.
evidence: This is a general observation about limitations of unsupervised clustering methods.

claim: Tissue segmentation utilizing pixel-by-pixel metabolite ratio data for imaging differential metabolic zones has not been reported to date.
source: To date, tissue segmentation utilizing pixel-by-pixel metabolite ratio data for imaging differential metabolic zones has not been reported.
evidence: This identifies a novel aspect of the current work.

claim: Metabolite/feature ratios may generate more meaningful biologically relevant ROIs due in part to reduction of systematic experimental noise.
source: We hypothesized that metabolite/feature ratios may generate more meaningful biologically relevant ROIs due in part to reduction of systematic experimental noise.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the manuscript.

claim: PCA analysis with ratios involving the top 5 components of 10 glutamate/glutamine-related metabolites generated an arc-shaped region that encompasses the hypothalamus, striatum and NAc, while non-ratio metabolite data did not.
source: As expected, consideration of 10 different glutamate/glutamine-related metabolites for PCA analysis (Supplementary file 3) with ratios involving the top 5 components generated an interesting arc-shaped region that encompasses the hypothalamus, striatum and NAc, while non-ratio metabolite data did not (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A more defined outline of striatum and cerebellum in the coronal brain structure was obtained in PCA segmentation using the top 5 component metabolite ratios as well as 5 LPEs but was not observed with these 5 LPEs alone.
source: Likewise, a more defined outline of striatum and cerebellum in the coronal brain structure was obtained in PCA segmentation using the top 5 component metabolite ratios as well as 5 LPEs Supplementary file 4 but was not observed with these 5 LPEs alone (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ratios among three neurotransmitter-related non-glutamate metabolites (glutamine, aspartate, and homocarnosine) show clear differences within the cerebral cortex for glutamine to aspartate ratios in COX10 KO and WT mouse brains.
source: In COX10 KO and WT mouse brains, ratios among three neurotransmitter-related non-glutamate metabolites (glutamine, aspartate, and homocarnosine) show clear differences within the cerebral cortex for glutamine to aspartate ratios (Figure 7A) and within the ventral striatum for homocarnosine to glutamine and homocarnosine to aspartate ratios (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ratio imaging data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Homocarnosine is a naturally occurring imidazole-containing dipeptide uniquely present in the brain, likely in a subclass of GABAergic neurons.
source: Homocarnosine is a naturally occurring imidazole-containing dipeptide uniquely present in the brain, likely in a subclass of GABAergic neurons (Rothman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Homocarnosine is synthetized from γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and histidine via homocarnosine synthase (CARNS1).
source: It is synthetized from γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and histidine via homocarnosine synthase (CARNS1) and can be hydrolyzed to histidine and GABA by carnosine dipeptidase 1 (CNDP1), which is exclusively expressed in brain (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: Homocarnosine can be hydrolyzed to histidine and GABA by carnosine dipeptidase 1 (CNDP1), which is exclusively expressed in brain.
source: It is synthetized from γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and histidine via homocarnosine synthase (CARNS1) and can be hydrolyzed to histidine and GABA by carnosine dipeptidase 1 (CNDP1), which is exclusively expressed in brain (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: Homocarnosine is recognized to play a role in mediating neuronal activity during satiation and starvation.
source: Homocarnosine is recognized to play a role in mediating neuronal activity during satiation and starvation (Filipović et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Homocarnosine is decreased in the brain during cold adaptation.
source: It is decreased in the brain during cold adaptation (Bondarenko et al., 1985) and increased during alcohol intoxication (Kukharenko et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Homocarnosine is increased in the brain during alcohol intoxication.
source: It is decreased in the brain during cold adaptation (Bondarenko et al., 1985) and increased during alcohol intoxication (Kukharenko et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Aspartate and glutamate can be exchanged across the inner mitochondrial membrane by mitochondrial carrier protein SLC25A12 (Aralar1).
source: Additionally, aspartate and glutamate can be exchanged across the inner mitochondrial membrane by mitochondrial carrier protein SLC25A12 (Aralar1), mainly distributed in brain and skeletal muscle for the transport of aspartate from mitochondria to cytosol, and in the transfer of cytosolic reducing equivalents into mitochondria as a member of the malate-aspartate shuttle (Jalil et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Brain function can be estimated from the ratio of glutamine to homocarnosine in cerebrospinal fluid.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that brain function can be estimated from the ratio of glutamine to homocarnosine in cerebrospinal fluid (Ohtsuka and Takahashi, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Homocarnosine is elevated in monkey brain in the setting of a protein-deficient diet, whereas aspartate and glutamate levels are unchanged.
source: An early report showed that homocarnosine is elevated in monkey brain in the setting of a protein-deficient diet, whereas aspartate and glutamate levels are unchanged (Enwonwu and Worthington, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In COX10 KO and WT brains, no difference in individual aspartate or glutamate levels was observed.
source: Similarly, in COX10 KO and WT brains, we observed no difference in individual aspartate or glutamate levels (Figure 5A–B), while striatal homocarnosine (Figure 7E) and glutamine (Figure 5C) were elevated.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Striatal homocarnosine and glutamine were elevated in COX10 KO brains.
source: Similarly, in COX10 KO and WT brains, we observed no difference in individual aspartate or glutamate levels (Figure 5A–B), while striatal homocarnosine (Figure 7E) and glutamine (Figure 5C) were elevated.
evidence: This is based on analysis of imaging data shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: An elevated homocarnosine to glutamine and glutamine to glutamate ratio could indicate increased synthesis of homocarnosine via the glutamine-glutamate-GABA axis in COX10 KO mice.
source: As COX10 KO mice displayed altered food intake, muscle mass and elevated starvation response (Southwell et al., 2023), an elevated homocarnosine to glutamine and glutamine to glutamate ratio (Figure 5F) could indicate increased synthesis of homocarnosine via the glutamine-glutamate-GABA axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on ratio imaging data and prior published findings.

claim: PCA results from ratios showed cyan blue located in larger areas of striatum and thalamus regions in KO relative to WT brains, while non-ratio PCA did not.
source: Comparing PCA overview images from ratio (Figure 7F) to non-ratio (Figure 7G), PCA results from ratios showed cyan blue located in larger areas of striatum and thalamus regions in KO relative to WT brains, while non-ratio PCA did not.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing PCA results in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: UMAP is a relatively newer non-linear dimension reduction algorithm often used to visualize complex dataset while preserving local structure.
source: Unlike PCA analysis, which builds on a linear dimension reduction algorithm, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) is a relatively newer non-linear dimension reduction algorithm often used to visualize complex dataset while preserving local structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about UMAP methodology.

claim: UMAP analysis of ratios for 5 LPEs in COX10 KO and WT murine brain sections, followed by K-mean clustering, showed much more defined and biologically relevant ROIs than those derived from non-ratioed LPEs.
source: UMAP analysis of ratios for 5 LPEs in COX10 KO and WT murine brain sections, followed by K-mean clustering, showed much more defined and biologically relevant ROIs than those derived from non-ratioed LPEs (Figure 8) that resemble PCA segmentation results (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing UMAP results in Figure 8.

claim: Non-ratio segmented ROIs did not provide comparable and confident ROIs among replicates.
source: While non-ratio segmented ROIs did not provide comparable and confident ROIs among replicates (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), the ratio-segmented data indicate a distinct LPE profile between the outer cortex (ROI 3), cortex (ROI 8), ventral thalamus (ROI 5) and striatal regions (ROI 2; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ratio-segmented data indicate a distinct LPE profile between the outer cortex, cortex, ventral thalamus and striatal regions.
source: While non-ratio segmented ROIs did not provide comparable and confident ROIs among replicates (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), the ratio-segmented data indicate a distinct LPE profile between the outer cortex (ROI 3), cortex (ROI 8), ventral thalamus (ROI 5) and striatal regions (ROI 2; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Murine brain imaging results showed decreased aspartate to NAA ratios visualizable in almost all 8 ROIs investigated with COX10 KO relative to WT, suggesting overall diminished expression or activity of NAT8L.
source: For example, murine brain imaging results showed decreased aspartate to NAA ratios visualizable in almost all 8 ROIs investigated with COX10 KO relative to WT, suggesting overall diminished expression or activity of NAT8L, the neuronal enzyme that produces NAA from acetyl-CoA and aspartate (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A-H).
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A-H.

claim: NAAG to NAA and aspartate ratios were greater in ROI 7 of KO compared to WT brain, suggesting elevated NAAG synthase activity in this defined region.
source: Moreover, NAAG, the most abundant dipeptide in the brain, can be synthesized from NAA and glutamate by NAAG synthase. NAAG to NAA and aspartate ratios were greater in ROI 7 of KO compared to WT brain (Figure 8—figure supplement 3I-J), suggesting elevated NAAG synthase activity in this defined region.
evidence: This is based on ratio imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3I-J.

claim: NAT8L mRNA oxidation is linked to neurodegeneration in multiple sclerosis.
source: Of note, NAT8L mRNA oxidation is linked to neurodegeneration in multiple sclerosis (Kharel et al., 2023) and overexpression-induced vulnerability to depressive behavior in mice (Uno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NAT8L overexpression induces vulnerability to depressive behavior in mice.
source: Of note, NAT8L mRNA oxidation is linked to neurodegeneration in multiple sclerosis (Kharel et al., 2023) and overexpression-induced vulnerability to depressive behavior in mice (Uno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NAAG functions as a retrograde neurotransmitter and is released in response to glutamate, providing postsynaptic neurons with a feedback mechanism to inhibit excessive glutamate signaling.
source: NAAG functions as a retrograde neurotransmitter and is released in response to glutamate, providing postsynaptic neurons with a feedback mechanism to inhibit excessive glutamate signaling (Morland and Nordengen, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The COX10 KO brain exhibits increased NAA and NAAG syntheses as feedback to inhibit excessive glutamate signaling.
source: Therefore, we infer that the COX10 KO brain exhibits increased NAA and NAAG syntheses as feedback to inhibit excessive glutamate signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ratio imaging data and known functions of NAAG.

claim: Glutamate within the NAc showed no change compared to WT, potentially due to excess glutamate being used for synthesis of glutamine and NAAG, which are elevated in KO ROI 7.
source: In contrast, glutamate within the NAc showed no change compared to WT, potentially due to excess glutamate being used for synthesis of glutamine and NAAG, which are elevated in KO ROI 7 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4C-D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: Glutamate to glutamine ratio positively correlated with glutamate, while negative correlations were observed for NAAG and NAAG/NAA in both WT and KO ROI 7.
source: Glutamate to glutamine ratio positively correlated with glutamate, while negative correlations were observed for NAAG and NAAG/NAA in both WT and KO ROI 7 (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of pixel data from ROI 7.

claim: UMAP generated ROIs are consistent with brain anatomy in horizonal and sagittal brain sections.
source: Given that LPE ratios can be used as a tool for brain segmentation and to overcome variations in section quality, we asked if UMAP with the same 5 LPE ratios can similarly be applied for other types of brain section ROI segmentation. As predicted, UMAP generated ROIs are consistent with brain anatomy in two separate experiments depicted by horizonal and sagittal brain sections (Figure 8—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 6.

claim: Analyses that utilize metabolite ratios are not a new concept in omics investigations, particularly for applications that involve medical MRI spectroscopy-generated imaging data.
source: Analyses that utilize metabolite ratios are not a new concept in omics investigations, particularly for applications that involve medical MRI spectroscopy-generated imaging data.
evidence: This acknowledges prior use of ratio analysis in other contexts.

claim: An unbiased strategy and application of pixel-by-pixel imaging of targeted and untargeted metabolite ratios for MSI data interpretation has been lacking.
source: Notwithstanding, an unbiased strategy and application of pixel-by-pixel imaging of targeted and untargeted metabolite ratios for MSI data interpretation has been lacking.
evidence: This identifies the novelty of the current work.

claim: Ratio imaging adds a powerful new tool to mitigate sample preparation artefacts, to spatially metabotype tissue microenvironments, and to reveal spatially distinct functional variations in enzymatic and metabolic pathway activities.
source: We demonstrate that ratio imaging adds a powerful new tool to mitigate sample preparation artefacts, to spatially metabotype tissue microenvironments, and to reveal spatially distinct functional variations in enzymatic and metabolic pathway activities.
evidence: This summarizes the main contributions demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Glutamate, glutamine, aspartate, histidine, homocarnosine and GABA are all well-recognized brain metabolites that contribute to fundamental brain activities, including synaptic transmission and energy production.
source: Glutamate, glutamine, aspartate, histidine, homocarnosine and GABA are all well-recognized brain metabolites that contribute to fundamental brain activities, including synaptic transmission and energy production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about brain metabolism.

claim: Ratios among glutamate, glutamine, aspartate, histidine, homocarnosine and GABA are tightly regulated for maintaining proper brain function and vary across different regions of the brain and under different physiological conditions.
source: Their ratios are tightly regulated for maintaining proper brain function and vary across different regions of the brain and under different physiological conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about brain metabolism.

claim: Disturbance of ratios among glutamate, glutamine, aspartate, histidine, homocarnosine and GABA can be deleterious to neurotransmission and overall brain health.
source: Disturbance of these ratios can be deleterious to neurotransmission and overall brain health.
evidence: This is established knowledge about brain metabolism.

claim: Untargeted pixel-by pixel ratios can be derived from all detected mass spectral features, irrespective of whether the features have known structural identities.
source: As described, untargeted pixel-by pixel ratios can be derived from all detected mass spectral features, irrespective of whether the features have known structural identities.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the approach.

claim: Information-rich metabolite ratio datasets offer great potential for association with other imaging or spatial omics data.
source: Combined with non-ratio feature data, information-rich metabolite ratio datasets offer great potential for association with other imaging or spatial omics data.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the approach.

claim: For pixel data with ≤10 µm raster width, single cell spatial imaging and omics data can ideally be associated with untargeted metabolite/feature ratio data to achieve single cell multiomics metadata integration.
source: For pixel data with ≤10 µm raster width, single cell spatial imaging and omics data can ideally be associated with untargeted metabolite/feature ratio data to achieve single cell multiomics metadata integration.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications at single-cell resolution.

claim: A potential challenge for single cell metabolomics spatial data interpretation lies in possible concerns regarding metabolite data co-registration with anatomical or other single cell omics datasets.
source: A potential challenge for single cell metabolomics spatial data interpretation lies in possible concerns regarding metabolite data co-registration with anatomical or other single cell omics datasets.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of single-cell spatial metabolomics.

claim: When datasets are obtained from serial sections, a mere 10 µm shift could result in cell layer disparities.
source: Notably, when datasets are obtained from serial sections, a mere 10 µm shift could result in cell layer disparities.
evidence: This describes a technical challenge in co-registration of serial sections.

claim: Combining ratio and non-ratio pixel data offers a powerful new tool to survey significant but unappreciated global correlations between metabolites ratios in distinct ROIs that are revealed by metabolite ratio tissue segmentation.
source: Combining ratio and non-ratio pixel data offers a powerful new tool to survey significant but unappreciated global correlations between metabolites ratios (both structurally defined and undefined) in distinct ROIs that are revealed by metabolite ratio tissue segmentation.
evidence: This summarizes a key application of the approach demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: An elevated glutamine to glutamate ratio is observed in COX10 KO brain compared to WT within the NAc and this ratio positively correlates with ferrous iron levels and Nat8L enzymatic activity.
source: Among other unexpected findings, we demonstrate that an elevated glutamine to glutamate ratio is observed in COX10 KO brain compared to WT within the NAc and that this ratio positively correlates with ferrous iron levels and Nat8L enzymatic activity (inferred from NAA to aspartate ratios, Table 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis and ratio imaging data.

claim: These associations were previously unrecognized but are consistent with a whole-body feed-forward action of mitochondrial myopathy on levels of brain leptin, corticosteroids, and neurotransmitter signaling.
source: These associations were previously unrecognized but are consistent with a whole-body feed-forward action of mitochondrial myopathy on levels of brain leptin, corticosteroids, and neurotransmitter signaling (Southwell et al., 2023).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior published work by the authors.

claim: The coverage of known metabolite structures and pathways is considerably less (typically 200–300 structurally identified species) for MSI than for LC/MS analyses.
source: One limitation for MSI ratio data interpretation is that the coverage of known metabolite structures and pathways is considerably less (typically 200–300 structurally identified species) than for LC/MS analyses.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of MSI compared to LC/MS.

claim: Combined ratio and non-ratio data can be used for segmentation, but segmentation results may be confounded by artefact-prone non-ratio metabolite data and thus not as clean as those using ratio alone.
source: It is important to note that combined ratio and non-ratio data can also be used for segmentation. However, segmentation results using combined ratio and non-ratio data may be confounded by artefact-prone non-ratio metabolite data and thus not as clean as those using ratio alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative results shown in the manuscript.

claim: Combining metabolite ratios from different metabolic pathways may segment tissue with ROIs more representative of real metabotypes.
source: We speculate that combining metabolite ratios from different metabolic pathways may segment tissue with ROIs more representative of real metabotypes.
evidence: This is a speculation about optimal segmentation strategies.

claim: Targeted and untargeted metabolite ratio imaging provides a powerful add-on tool for MSI experiments, revealing otherwise hidden information in acquired datasets.
source: In summary, we anticipate targeted and untargeted metabolite ratio imaging to provide a powerful add-on tool for MSI experiments, revealing otherwise hidden information in acquired datasets.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the utility of the approach.

claim: Metabolite ratios may serve as potential new biomarkers to distinguish anatomically distinct metabolic tissue regions and uncover otherwise unrecognized differences in either physiological cell function or from differing cellular responses to drug treatments and disease states.
source: These ratios may serve as potential new biomarkers to distinguish anatomically distinct metabolic tissue regions and uncover otherwise unrecognized differences in either physiological cell function or from differing cellular responses to drug treatments and disease states.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of ratio imaging.

claim: The ratio imaging strategy can be extended to image pixel-by-pixel fractional abundance of isotopologues for targeted and untargeted MALDI-MSI stable isotope tracing.
source: This ratio imaging strategy can be further extended to image pixel-by-pixel fractional abundance of isotopologues for targeted and untargeted MALDI-MSI stable isotope tracing.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the approach.

claim: When coupled with the FT-ICR high resolution mass spectrometer, simultaneous imaging of isotopologue incorporation is possible for tracing molecules containing mixed stable isotope elements.
source: When coupled with the FT-ICR high resolution mass spectrometer, simultaneous imaging of isotopologue incorporation is possible for tracing molecules containing mixed stable isotope elements (e.g. 13C, 15N, 2H, 18O, 34S).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications with high-resolution MS.
